cards.question: In one phrase, what is a thread?
cards.answer: An independent execution context (stream of instructions) within a single process.

cards.question: In the toy-shop analogy, what does a "thread" correspond to?
cards.answer: A worker in the toy shop (active, works simultaneously with others, needs coordination).

cards.question: Why must a process have multiple threads to use multiple CPUs/cores?
cards.answer: A single execution context (one PC/stack/registers) can only run on one CPU at a time.

cards.question: What do threads in the same process share?
cards.answer: The entire virtual address space (code, data, file mappings).

cards.question: What per-thread state must each thread keep separate, even though it shares an address space?
cards.answer: Its own program counter, stack pointer, stack, and registers.

cards.question: How does a multithreaded process's PCB differ from a single-threaded one?
cards.answer: One shared section (address space, code/data) plus separate per-thread execution-context info for each thread.

cards.question: Do threads or processes usually result in hotter caches when several execute concurrently?
cards.answer: Threads — since they share an address space, one thread's cached data is often useful to another.

cards.question: Why do threads context-switch faster than processes?
cards.answer: They share the same virtual-to-physical mappings, so no new address-space mapping has to be created.

cards.question: Do both processes and threads have their own execution context (stack + registers)?
cards.answer: Yes — both do.

cards.question: Do both processes and threads use some communication mechanism between execution contexts?
cards.answer: Yes — processes use IPC; threads synchronize via shared memory.

cards.question: Give 2 reasons multithreading is more resource-efficient than an equivalent multi-process design.
cards.answer: Threads share one address space (no duplicate memory allocation) and communicate via shared memory instead of costlier IPC.

cards.question: How does splitting work across specialized threads (vs. generic ones) improve performance?
cards.answer: Each thread repeatedly touches a smaller code/data footprint, so it runs with a hotter cache.

cards.question: Why is multithreading useful even on a single CPU?
cards.answer: It lets the CPU switch to another thread during one thread's I/O wait, hiding idle time.

cards.question: Under what condition does it make sense to switch to another thread instead of just waiting on I/O?
cards.answer: When the expected idle time exceeds roughly 2x the context-switch cost.

cards.question: Why is hiding I/O latency cheaper with threads than with processes?
cards.answer: Thread context switches skip recreating virtual-to-physical address mappings, so they're faster.

cards.question: How does multithreading benefit the OS kernel itself?
cards.answer: Lets the kernel run multiple execution contexts concurrently across CPUs (e.g. for daemons/drivers).

cards.question: In Birrell's thread model, what does the thread data structure store?
cards.answer: Thread ID, register values (PC, stack pointer), the stack, and other thread-specific attributes.

cards.question: In Birrell's model, what 2 arguments does thread fork() take?
cards.answer: A procedure to run (proc) and its arguments (args).

cards.question: After a Birrell-style fork() creates thread T1, what does the parent thread do next?
cards.answer: Continues executing the instruction right after the fork call, concurrently with T1.

cards.question: What does join() do in Birrell's thread model?
cards.answer: Blocks the calling thread until the specified child thread finishes, then returns its result.

cards.question: Once a joined child thread finishes, what happens to its resources?
cards.answer: They're freed and the child is terminated.

cards.question: Why do concurrently running threads risk data races even though processes don't (by default)?
cards.answer: Threads share the same virtual-to-physical mappings, so they can legally access the exact same memory at the same time.

cards.question: What is mutual exclusion?
cards.answer: A guarantee that only one thread at a time can execute a given operation/section of code.

cards.question: What is a mutex?
cards.answer: A lock construct that gives one thread at a time exclusive access to a shared resource.

cards.question: What happens to a thread that tries to lock an already-locked mutex?
cards.answer: It blocks (suspends) until the mutex is released.

cards.question: What does a mutex data structure need to track?
cards.answer: Its lock state (locked/free), the list of threads blocked on it, and (often) its current owner.

cards.question: What is a "critical section"?
cards.answer: The portion of code protected by a mutex, where only one thread may execute at a time.

cards.question: In a mutex API with separate lock()/unlock() calls, what must a programmer remember to do?
cards.answer: Explicitly call unlock() when leaving the critical section, or no other thread can proceed.

cards.question: What problem do condition variables solve that plain mutexes can't?
cards.answer: Letting a thread wait efficiently until a specific condition becomes true, instead of busy-waiting/polling.

cards.question: What 2 arguments does a condition variable's wait() call take?
cards.answer: A mutex and a condition variable.

cards.question: What does wait() do to the mutex it's called with?
cards.answer: Automatically releases it while waiting, and automatically reacquires it before returning.

cards.question: What's the difference between signal() and broadcast() on a condition variable?
cards.answer: signal() wakes one waiting thread; broadcast() wakes all waiting threads.

cards.question: After broadcast() wakes multiple threads, can they all proceed immediately?
cards.answer: No — they must reacquire the shared mutex one at a time.

cards.question: Why must a condition-variable wait always be inside a while loop (not an if)?
cards.answer: The predicate must be rechecked after waking, since the shared state may have changed again before this thread resumes.

cards.question: What is the readers/writer problem?
cards.answer: Letting any number of readers access a resource concurrently, but only one writer (and no readers) at a time.

cards.question: Why can't a plain mutex alone solve the readers/writer problem?
cards.answer: A mutex only allows one thread at a time total — it can't allow multiple concurrent readers.

cards.question: In the readers/writer solution, what does the resource_counter proxy variable's value mean?
cards.answer: 0 = free, positive N = N active readers, -1 = one active writer.

cards.question: In the readers/writer solution, what do the read_phase and write_phase condition variables represent?
cards.answer: What waiting readers, and waiting writers, block on respectively.

cards.question: In the readers/writer solution, why does the last exiting reader signal write_phase (not broadcast)?
cards.answer: Only one writer can proceed, so waking just one waiter is correct.

cards.question: In the readers/writer solution, why does an exiting writer broadcast to read_phase?
cards.answer: Multiple readers can proceed concurrently, so all waiting readers should be woken.

cards.question: What's the standard structure of an "enter critical section" block?
cards.answer: Lock mutex → check predicate in a while loop → wait if not met → proceed once met.

cards.question: What's the standard structure of an "exit critical section" block?
cards.answer: Lock mutex → update shared state/predicate → signal/broadcast → unlock.

cards.question: Common pitfall: what should you do when declaring a mutex/condition variable?
cards.answer: Comment which shared resource/operation it protects.

cards.question: Common pitfall: what happens if different threads use different mutexes to protect the same resource?
cards.answer: The mutex offers no real protection — concurrent unsafe access can still happen.

cards.question: Common pitfall: is calling broadcast() when signal() would suffice dangerous?
cards.answer: No — just less efficient. Using signal() when broadcast() was needed IS dangerous (threads can wait forever).

cards.question: What is a "spurious wake-up"?
cards.answer: A thread woken by signal/broadcast that still can't proceed (e.g. mutex still held), wasting a context switch.

cards.question: How can spurious wake-ups sometimes be avoided?
cards.answer: Unlock the mutex before calling signal/broadcast, when correctness allows it.

cards.question: What is a deadlock?
cards.answer: A situation where two or more threads each wait on a resource the other holds, so none can proceed.

cards.question: In the classic 2-thread/2-mutex deadlock, what causes it?
cards.answer: T1 locks A then wants B, while T2 locks B then wants A — a circular wait.

cards.question: What graph condition is necessary and sufficient for a deadlock?
cards.answer: A cycle in the wait-for graph (edges from a waiting thread to the thread holding what it needs).

cards.question: What's the standard foolproof way to prevent deadlocks?
cards.answer: Enforce a global lock ordering — always acquire mutexes in the same order.

cards.question: Besides prevention, what are 2 other strategies for dealing with deadlocks?
cards.answer: Detect + roll back and recover, or do nothing and hope (the "ostrich algorithm").

cards.question: Why is deadlock detection + rollback often impractical?
cards.answer: It's expensive, and some operations (e.g. external I/O) can't be rolled back.

cards.question: What's the difference between a kernel-level thread and a user-level thread?
cards.answer: Kernel-level threads are visible to and scheduled by the OS; user-level threads are managed by a library and invisible to the OS unless mapped.

cards.question: What must happen before a user-level thread can actually execute on a CPU?
cards.answer: It must be associated with a kernel-level thread, which the OS scheduler then schedules.

cards.question: Describe the One-to-One threading model.
cards.answer: Each user-level thread maps to its own kernel-level thread.

cards.question: What's the main benefit of the One-to-One model?
cards.answer: The OS sees all threads, so it can schedule/manage them with full native support.

cards.question: What's the main downside of the One-to-One model?
cards.answer: Every thread operation costs a system call, and you're limited by kernel-imposed policies/limits.

cards.question: Describe the Many-to-One threading model.
cards.answer: All user-level threads map onto a single kernel-level thread.

cards.question: What's the main benefit of the Many-to-One model?
cards.answer: Fully portable — all scheduling/sync happens in user space, no system calls needed.

cards.question: What's the main downside of the Many-to-One model?
cards.answer: If one user-level thread blocks (e.g. on I/O), the whole process stalls.

cards.question: Describe the Many-to-Many threading model.
cards.answer: Multiple user-level threads map onto multiple kernel-level threads (not strictly 1:1).

cards.question: What's the main benefit of Many-to-Many over Many-to-One?
cards.answer: If one user thread blocks, other kernel threads remain available so the process can still progress.

cards.question: In the Many-to-Many model, what is a "bound" thread?
cards.answer: A user-level thread permanently, one-to-one mapped to a specific kernel-level thread (e.g. for responsiveness/priority).

cards.question: What's the main downside of the Many-to-Many model?
cards.answer: It requires extra coordination between the kernel-level and user-level thread managers.

cards.question: What is "process scope" thread management?
cards.answer: A user-level thread library manages/schedules threads only within its own process; the OS is unaware of them.

cards.question: What is "system scope" thread management?
cards.answer: The OS-level scheduler manages threads across the entire platform, seeing every thread.

cards.question: With process-scope threading, if two processes have very different thread counts, how does the OS typically split CPU between them?
cards.answer: Roughly evenly per-process, regardless of thread count — so the process with more threads gets less CPU per thread.

cards.question: Describe the boss-workers pattern.
cards.answer: One boss thread accepts/assigns work; worker threads each perform the entire task.

cards.question: In the boss-workers pattern, what limits system throughput?
cards.answer: The time the boss spends handling each incoming request.

cards.question: What's the preferred way for the boss to hand off work, and why?
cards.answer: A shared producer-consumer queue — avoids the boss tracking worker status or waiting on a handshake.

cards.question: Why use a dynamically-sized thread pool instead of creating a worker per request?
cards.answer: Avoids the latency of creating a new thread on demand, while avoiding a wastefully fixed pool size.

cards.question: What's the main downside of the (unspecialized) boss-workers pattern?
cards.answer: It ignores locality — the boss doesn't consider which worker's cache already holds relevant state.

cards.question: How does specializing workers by task type improve the boss-workers pattern?
cards.answer: Better cache locality (smaller data footprint per thread) and lets it prioritize certain task types.

cards.question: What's the main added cost of a specialized-worker boss-workers variant?
cards.answer: More complex load balancing across worker groups.

cards.question: Describe the pipeline pattern.
cards.answer: The overall task is split into ordered stages; each stage is handled by a dedicated thread (or pool), and work flows through the stages.

cards.question: What determines a pipeline's overall throughput?
cards.answer: Its slowest stage (bottleneck).

cards.question: How do you fix a pipeline stage that's slower than the others?
cards.answer: Assign it multiple threads (a small thread pool for that stage).

cards.question: How should work be passed between pipeline stages?
cards.answer: Via a shared buffer/queue between adjacent stages, not direct hand-offs.

cards.question: What's the main benefit of the pipeline pattern?
cards.answer: Highly specialized threads per stage → better cache locality/efficiency.

cards.question: What's the main downside of the pipeline pattern?
cards.answer: Complex to keep balanced as workload/resources change, plus more synchronization points.

cards.question: Describe the layered pattern.
cards.answer: Related tasks are grouped into layers; a request passes up/down through the layers, and any thread in a layer can handle its subtasks.

cards.question: How does the layered pattern differ from the pipeline pattern in how work flows?
cards.answer: Work can pass in both directions through layers, not just forward through stages.

cards.question: What's the main downside of the layered pattern?
cards.answer: More complex synchronization (each layer coordinates with the ones above and below), and it may not suit all applications.

cards.question: Is Birrell's fork() the same as UNIX fork()?
cards.answer: No. Birrell's creates a thread; UNIX's copies a process.
cards.memory: Same name, different animal.

cards.question: Why is join() unnecessary in the safe_insert example?
cards.answer: The result is already visible in the shared list.
cards.memory: join is for getting results; here they're already shared.

cards.question: What goes wrong if two threads insert at the head of a list concurrently?
cards.answer: Both read the same head, so one insert is lost.
cards.memory: Race: both write p_next = old head; the last writer wins.

cards.question: Mutex quiz: T2 and T4 are waiting when T1 unlocks, and T5 arrives just then. Who can get the lock?
cards.answer: T2, T4, or T5.
cards.memory: No FIFO guarantee: a newcomer can win.

cards.question: In producer/consumer without a CV, what does the consumer do?
cards.answer: Busy-waits: lock, check if full, unlock, repeat.
cards.memory: "Are we there yet?"

cards.question: When does a producer signal list_full?
cards.answer: Only when its insert made the list full.
cards.memory: Only ring the bell when there's news.

cards.question: wait() implementation step 1?
cards.answer: Release the mutex and join the CV's wait queue.
cards.memory: Release the key, then take a seat in the waiting room.

cards.question: wait() implementation step 2 (on signal)?
cards.answer: Leave the queue and reacquire the mutex, then return.
cards.memory: Hand back the key while you nap; grab it again on waking.

cards.question: Why is broadcast sometimes not very useful?
cards.answer: Woken threads still take the mutex one at a time.
cards.memory: Everyone wakes, but there's still one key.

cards.question: CV quiz: why use while instead of if?
cards.answer: The list may change before the consumer reacquires the mutex (all of the above).
cards.memory: Wake-up means "maybe"; the while loop checks again.

cards.question: Toy shop quiz: what is the new-order entry predicate?
cards.answer: while (new_order == 3 || (new_order == 1 && old_order > 0)) wait
cards.memory: Up to 3 new orders; old orders only allowed while ≤ 1 new order.

cards.question: Toy shop quiz: is `if` instead of `while` correct?
cards.answer: No. Another thread may change the counts first.
cards.memory: if = trust the old news; while = check again.

cards.question: Toy shop quiz: is `new_order >= 3` also correct?
cards.answer: Yes. new_order can never exceed 3.
cards.memory: Can't exceed 3, so ≥ 3 behaves the same as == 3.

cards.question: Does signaling one CV before another give it priority?
cards.answer: No. The scheduler decides who runs first.
cards.memory: Code order ≠ run order.

cards.question: Deadlock fix: why doesn't fine-grained locking (unlock A, then lock B) work?
cards.answer: The code needs A and B held together.
cards.memory: Fine-grained only works if you need one lock at a time.

cards.question: Deadlock fix: what does one mega-lock for A and B cost?
cards.answer: Parallelism: only one thread at a time.
cards.memory: One giant lock = one thread at a time.

cards.question: What do the deadlock-handling techniques have in common?
cards.answer: They're expensive; used mostly in performance-critical systems.
cards.memory: Prevention and detection cost a lot; lock order is the cheap fix.

cards.question: Toy shop: which step does the boss do in boss-workers?
cards.answer: Only step 1 (accept the order).
cards.memory: The boss hands off immediately to stay fast.

cards.question: Boss-worker handshake: pro?
cards.answer: Workers don't need to synchronize with each other.
cards.memory: Each worker gets its own direct order: no tray fights.

cards.question: Boss-worker handshake: con?
cards.answer: The boss tracks and waits on workers, so throughput drops.
cards.memory: The boss becomes a babysitter.

cards.question: Boss-worker: what happens when the shared queue is full?
cards.answer: The boss waits, so throughput drops.
cards.memory: Full tray → the boss stands and waits.

cards.question: Boss-worker pool: how does it grow?
cards.answer: Several threads at a time, not one per request.
cards.memory: Hire in batches.

cards.question: Layered pattern: what is its benefit over a pipeline?
cards.answer: Coarser, so choosing threads per layer is easier.
cards.memory: Fewer, bigger groups = fewer sizing decisions.

cards.question: Specialized threads: what else can you do with them besides locality?
cards.answer: Give important tasks or customers higher priority.
cards.memory: VIP customers get more workers.

cards.question: Kernel-level threads: what else do they run besides user threads?
cards.answer: OS services such as daemons and drivers.
cards.memory: The kernel has its own staff too.
